1:
Clarke lays out the whole chapter at the start: a king of Tyre whose pretensions the prophet treats with severe irony, then a funeral dirge in which his former pomp is finely contrasted with his fall, in terms that seem frequently to allude to the fall of Lucifer; then the overthrow of Sidon, the mother city of Tyre; and finally a promise to the Jews of deliverance. Keil and Delitzsch note the same shape from the preceding chapters, that as the city was first threatened with destruction and then her fall confirmed by a lamentation, so the prince is first forewarned of his death and then lamented. Gill marks only that the prophecy turns from the city to its king.

Who the king was is disputed. Clarke lists the candidates: some think Hiram, some the devil, others Ithobaal, with whom he says the chronology and circumstances best agree, while Origen thought the guardian angel of the city was intended. Gill gives the name as Ethbaal or Ithobalus after Josephus, and dismisses as a fable of the Jewish rabbins, reported by Jerom, the notion that this was the Hiram of the days of Solomon living a thousand years; but he keeps a figural reading, holding the prince an emblem not so much of the devil as of antichrist.

The charge is pride, and the voices differ over how literally to take it. Henry has him not only think it but speak it out with impudence, and works out what the claim amounted to: he thought the city had as necessary a dependence on him as the world has upon the God that made it, that he was independent and unaccountable, and that he had as much wisdom and authority as God himself, his word being as much a law. Henry adds that God has indeed said of princes that they are gods, but that it does not become them to say so of themselves, being a high affront to him who is God alone and will not give his glory to another. Ellicott takes the opposite line: it is not to be supposed that the king actually claimed religious homage, as some monarchs and later emperors did, but that he had a proud sense of elevation and self-sufficiency which is only translated into words by the text. Wesley too puts the saying in the heart. Ellicott calls the condition the insanity of prosperity and lists instances, from Sennacherib and the reigning king of Babylon, to whom he says this prophecy might well have served as a warning, through Pharaoh and Herod to more modern conquerors and many who, being eminently successful in other walks of life, have sacrificed to their own net.

The seat of God is given a local sense. Ellicott holds the phrase chosen not merely for the beauty and apparently impregnable position of Tyre but for its being called the holy island and looked to by its colonies as the central sanctuary of their worship, the temple of Melkarth being dated by its priests to nearly three thousand years before and called by Arrian the oldest sanctuary in the annals of mankind. Wesley reads it more simply as safe and impregnable as heaven itself, and sets against it that a man is subject to casualties, sorrows and distresses. On the comparison with Daniel all agree the words are ironical, Clarke noting that Daniel was then living and reputable for his great wisdom, and Ellicott that he was so famed throughout the empire that the report must have reached Tyre, having been twenty years at court when Jerusalem fell, five years before the siege of Tyre began. Gill reports that the Septuagint, Syriac and Arabic versions render the clause as a question instead, asking whether he is not wiser than Daniel, then famous throughout Chaldea for his skill in government and in the interpreting of dreams.
4:
The wealth and its source are the first matter. Gill has the Tyrians and their princes famous for skill in navigation and trade, by which they acquired great wealth, and renders the second clause as wisdom exercised in traffic rather than wisdom alongside it. Clarke turns the same fact into the charge: the king attributed everything to himself and did not acknowledge a divine providence, so that as he got all by himself he believed he could keep all by himself and had no need of any foreign help. Ellicott simply restates the arraignment, that the man entertained thoughts and purposes fitting only to the Supreme.

The sentence brings strangers. Gill and Clarke both name the Chaldean army, Gill adding that they not only lived at a distance from Tyre but were unknown to it, having no trade with it and appearing nowhere among the merchants of Tyre. Ellicott is less certain, noting that though the phrase rendered the terrible of the nations is used of the Chaldeans elsewhere in the book, the term is by no means necessarily confined to them; and he explains the odd figure of swords drawn against the beauty of wisdom by observing that the expression is only a way of designating Tyre itself, where Wesley takes it for the beautiful things in which the wisdom of the king appeared.

The death is described three times over. Gill takes the pit for the grave, the pit of corruption and destruction, and Ellicott notes that the plural in the following clause reproduces a rare form of the original and emphatically indicates a violent death. On the taunt that follows, Gill calls it a bitter sarcasm, asking whether a man in the hands of his enemies and about to be put to death will still assert his deity to the face of his killer, and Clarke asks whether he will keep his arrogance when the sword is sheathed in him. Ellicott corrects the rendering here: the future supplied in italics should be dropped, the form being exactly that of the earlier verse and best translated the same way, so that the contrast comes out plainly between the weakness of man and the power of God. Gill, Clarke and Wesley all read the deaths of the uncircumcised as two, temporal and eternal, Gill citing the Targum for the death of the wicked and Clarke adding that the king was taken and killed by Nebuchadnezzar. Ellicott reads the word rather for its force than its number, holding that to a Jew it carried all and more than all the opprobrium the Greeks and Romans attached to barbarians, so that it amounts to calling him profane and impious. He closes by pointing forward, that what follows represents the prince as like the first man, perfect and placed in Eden until his fall drives him ignominiously out, and that the passage is strongly ironical.
11:
The turn from prince to king raises the largest question in the chapter. Gill notes only that after the ruin of the prince the prophet is ordered to take up a lamentation on the king, and Henry sets the pattern from the preceding chapters, that as the prediction of the ruin of Tyre was followed by a pathetic lamentation, so the ruin of the king, once foretold, is bewailed. Henry then reports what the expositors have made of the change of title. It is commonly understood of the prince then reigning, whom he names Ethbaal or Ithobalus after Diodorus Siculus, an accomplished man upon all external accounts, very great and famous, whose iniquity was his ruin. Some, he says, take the king of Tyre for the whole royal family, taking in the foregoing kings and looking as far back as Hiram, and note that the then governor is called prince while the one lamented here is called king.

Beyond the literal sense the readings divide three ways. Many expositors, Henry reports, find an allegory alluding to the fall of the angels that sinned and undid themselves by their pride, some passages referring primarily to the king, as that of his merchandise, and others to the angels, as that of being in the holy mountain of God. Henry himself, if there is anything mystical in it, would rather refer it to the fall of Adam, which he thinks glanced at in the mention of Eden. Gill reports both readings without deciding, and adds that several passages of the chapter are interpreted of Adam in the Talmud. Clarke takes the comparison as strong irony, that the king is like Adam when in his innocence and excellence he was in the garden. Gill guards the literal ground: the king was never in Eden, but his situation in Tyre was as safe and pleasant and delightful as that of Adam in the garden, at least in his own imagination.

The opening phrase of the lamentation is rendered three ways. Clarke reports and endorses a translation that makes it thou drawest thy own likeness, so that the king forms a portrait of himself and represents himself the perfection of wisdom and beauty. Ellicott takes it more soberly as marking something complete or perfect, and notes that the word rendered sum occurs only once elsewhere, where it describes the well measured and arranged building of the temple. Wesley reads it as self-deception, that the king fancies fulness of wisdom and perfection of beauty to be in him.

The ornaments are handled with some care. Ellicott allows uncertainty over the names of the stones, since one rendered sardius may be carnelian and another beryl may be chrysolite, but takes the general point as an allusion to the profuse use of precious stones in the royal apparel of eastern monarchs; he observes that they are the same as the stones in the breastplate of the high priest with the third row omitted, which the Greek supplies. On the last clause he differs sharply from Wesley. Ellicott holds that the word rendered pipes occurs only here and most probably means females, those who played upon the tambourines, whereas Wesley hears instruments, the lute and tabret sounding both loud and softer music on the day of a coronation, all of them of most exquisite make and the work of their own artists. Ellicott adds a point that fits his Adam reading, that none of these things had to be collected by the king but stood ready prepared to his hand at his accession, just as everything was made ready for Adam in Eden; Wesley likewise glosses the day of creation as the day of coronation.
14:
The cherub is placed differently by each voice. Gill takes the allusion to be to the cherubim over the mercy seat, which covered it with their wings and were anointed as the ark and all the vessels of the tabernacle were, and reads the three terms in order: cherub for wisdom and power, anointed for royal dignity, that covereth for the office of protecting his people, all of which he either was, or ought to have been, or supposed himself to be; he adds that the Targum understands the whole of regal power. Clarke offers the gate of Paradise as well, likening the king to the cherub that guarded it and kept the way of the tree of life, or else to one of those whose wings covered the mercy seat. Ellicott traces the imagery to the temple upon Mount Zion, not because the king had any connection with it but because those terms came naturally to the prophet in an ironical description; the holy mountain, he says, is spoken of Tyre as a venerated sanctuary rising up from the sea. He also corrects the tense, since the Hebrew does not express it and the simple past used throughout the passage should be supplied here too. Wesley reads the cherub of wisdom and excellency, the anointing of the sacredness of the office, and the covering of the exercise of power as a shield to the weak, and hears in the added clause a rebuke, that it was God, whom the king forgets, who made him so.

The stones of fire divide them further. Clarke takes them for floors paved with precious stones that shone and sparkled like fire, and quotes a Latin poet describing the apartments of Cleopatra in nearly the same language, with golden plates in the beams, walls of solid marble, onyx underfoot, posts of ebony brought from Meroe and doors of polished tortoise. Wesley reads them simply as stones sparkling like fire about the king. Ellicott rejects the obvious explanation, that they are the brilliant jewels on the robes in which the king walked, since on that reading the expression would be a strange one and the connection implies a deeper and religious meaning; he prefers to see the paved work of sapphire beneath the feet of God, whose glory is like a devouring fire, making this one more way in which the king is ironically shown assuming attributes that are not his. Clarke reports a further view, that the stones of fire are the stars, on which the whole passage would refer to the fall of Satan.

The fall itself is read as Adam again. Ellicott says the comparison is renewed still more clearly here, the king altogether prosperous until his sin became manifest and then, his heart corrupted by his prosperity, cast out for ever as Adam was from his paradise; Clarke keeps the irony to the end, that the king had been like the angels, like Moses, like the cherubs, like Adam, like God, until his iniquity was found out. Ellicott notices that the language passes from the king to the state over which he presided and with which he was identified, and then returns to him personally, so that it is he who is cast out of his imagined mountain, he the covering cherub who is destroyed, and his fancied walking amid the stones of fire that ceases for ever. Gill has the merchandise reach the several nations that came to the markets and fairs of Tyre and to whom she sent her goods, and takes the lifting up of the heart to be over riches, wealth, power and authority; Wesley glosses the corruption as a depraving or losing of wisdom, and the laying of the man before kings as making him a spectacle and a warning to them.
18:
What the defiled sanctuaries are is disputed. Gill offers two senses, either the palaces of the king and his nobles, as Kimchi renders the word, where much iniquity was committed and which were therefore destroyed by the Chaldeans, or the places where their gods were worshipped. Ellicott holds that they are not so much the actual temples of Tyre as the ideal holy mountain of God in which the prince was figured as a covering cherub, though he grants that in the other sense too the Tyrians did not act up to the religious light they had, and by violating their consciences defiled even such representation of true religion as survived in their idolatrous worship; he adds that many Hebrew manuscripts have the singular. Clarke keeps the irony running: as God, as the angels, as the cherubim, the king must have had his sanctuaries and has defiled them, and as Adam he has polluted his Eden and been expelled. On the iniquity of the traffic Ellicott draws a general rule, that the sin consists in the abuse of the very blessings God had given and leads directly to its own punishment, no fact being more striking in the history of Israel or of the heathen than that the gifts of God are perverted by man, first to guilt and then to ruin.

The end is described briefly. Wesley has the king burnt to ashes and trampled under foot. Gill puts the astonishment in the contrast, that so mighty a city and so powerful a prince should be destroyed at once and brought from such prosperity to so low an estate, to the amazement of the kings and merchants who knew them; Wesley names the same witnesses, all who had known his riches, power, allies and wisdom. Clarke sharpens it to a reversal, that instead of an object of adoration he becomes a subject of horror and is destroyed with his city so that nothing but his name remains; the city, he notes, was entirely burnt by Alexander the Great as it had been before by Nebuchadnezzar.

A separate prophecy then turns to Zidon, and the voices explain why it needed one. Gill and Henry both place it near Tyre and in confederacy with it, Henry adding that it was the more ancient but not so considerable, had a dependence upon it, and stood and fell with it. Ellicott says there are several obvious reasons for a word directed especially against Zidon besides making up the number of the nations to seven, though she belonged to the same people and furnished mariners to Tyre. Henry finds the reason in her religion: the Zidonians seem to have been more addicted to idolatry than the Tyrians, who, being men of business and large conversation, were less under the power of bigotry, and they were noted for a worship that a king of Israel introduced and that the daughter of a king of Zidon brought in with the worship of Baal. Being borderers on the land where God was known, they might have learned to glorify him, and seduced Israel to their idols instead.

The purpose of the judgment is stated plainly. Henry takes the glory of God for his great end in all the good and all the evil that proceed out of the mouth of the Most High, and reads the doubled formula as one, since when God is sanctified he is glorified, his holiness being his glory; those who would not know by gentler methods shall be made to know that he is the Lord, and a just and jealous God, when destroying judgments have been executed according to the sentence passed. Keil and Delitzsch put the point historically, that the Lord will glorify himself upon Sidon as he did before upon Pharaoh, an unusual word here evidently pointing back to that deliverance, the glorification being effected by the judgments themselves.
22:
Zidon is placed before it is judged. Clarke gives its history: it had long possessed the empire of the sea and of all Phoenicia, and Tyre was one of its colonies, though in process of time the daughter became greater than the mother; it seems to have been independent when Tyre was taken, but was likely taken by the Chaldeans soon after. Wesley locates it north-west of Canaan, a royal seat of old from which Tyre descended. Gill takes the preface of the divine name as assuring the fulfilment and as set against the gods of the Zidonians, and Wesley unfolds the two verbs, that the judgments will make justice, power and truth appear so that all shall confess the glory, and that to be sanctified is to be owned as holy, reverenced as just and obeyed as sovereign. On the judgment itself Gill pairs the plague and the sword as two sore judgments that often go together, the one slaying those within and the other those the enemy meets in the streets, while Clarke takes the wounded for the soldiery, so that all supports are removed and the defenders destroyed.

The brier and the thorn are read historically and prophetically. Clarke suspects an allusion to the daughter of a king of Sidon who married a king of Israel and became the universal restorer of idolatry in the land, so that with Sidon destroyed no encourager of idolatry would come from that quarter. Wesley makes the two metaphors stand for the troublesome neighbours of the Jews generally, naming Moab, Ammon, Edom, Tyre and Zidon, and holds that the promise never had a full accomplishment yet but will, since the scripture cannot be broken. Ellicott traces the language back to an older threat of which Israel had long had bitter experience, and makes two observations about the brevity of this oracle: nothing is said of the special sins of Zidon and very little of the detail of her overthrow, these being already known or covered by what was said of Tyre, and no such utter desolation is foretold of her as of the greater city.

The closing promise divides on its date. Gill denies that the gathering is the return from the captivity in Babylon, since the ten tribes did not then return, though a few of them may have done so as a pledge of what should come, and places it in the latter day. Clarke keeps it historical and reads the whole sequence of judgments as preparation: during the long captivity God was making the land a safe dwelling, executing judgment on the heathen nations round about by the hand of the Chaldeans, so that Tyre and Sidon fell along with the Ammonites and the other inveterate enemies of the Jews; judgment began at his own house, proceeded to the nations, and only when they were brought down did he visit and redeem his people, by which the ways of God are proved all equal, partialities and caprices belonging not to him. Ellicott marks the same order of providence, the judgment on Judah having already come in the fall of the holy city, leading them to repentance so that God is sanctified in the sight of the heathen, then the promise of return, then judgment on the enemies who despised them, and then peace; and though the immediate point is the return of the Jews to their own land, he takes the long struggle between them and their enemies as one between the church of God and the powers of the world, so that the promise of rest looks forward in some sense to a final victory over all evil. Wesley puts it more simply, that God was dishonoured by his people in the sight of the heathen and will be honoured by them in the same sight, and Gill closes with none left to make them afraid.
